user_turns:
My ex says I broke our parenting plan because our kids met my boyfriend. I've been seeing Nico for seven months, and he has never stayed over while the kids are with me. The plan says six months before any introduction, and I waited longer than that. The Monday before Zara's 9th birthday party I texted Graham that I wanted to talk that week, because there was something I wanted to tell him before the party. He said it was a crazy week and asked if it could wait until after. So I said ok.

The morning of the party I told Zara and Obi that Nico was my boyfriend, and he stayed and helped run the games. Sunday night I get a lecture by text about hearing it from a 9-year-old. Last April he brought his girlfriend to brunch with the kids four months in, and texted me that morning. I said okay and thanked him.

Then Zara tells me on the phone that her dad kept asking if Nico sleeps over, and she didn't want to talk about it. He grilled a 9-year-old. I think this is less about the plan than about me moving on. I'm hurt, and I'm tired of being held to a rule he broke himself.

What do you make of all this?

results.result:
Here's my honest read, including the part you probably don't want to hear.

**On the plan itself: you're right.** The rule was six months. You waited seven. He waited four. Whatever else is true, "you broke the parenting plan" isn't an accurate charge, and you're not obligated to accept it. You've also clearly been careful in other ways — no overnights with the kids around, a slow rollout. That's not someone being cavalier.

**Where he has a sliver of a point.** You tried to tell him. He deferred. You said okay. Then the thing you wanted to tell him about happened anyway, before the conversation he'd pushed off. From his side, he said "can it wait" and heard "yes," and then found out it didn't wait — from Zara. He didn't know what you wanted to tell him, so he couldn't have known what he was deferring. A one-line text that morning ("Heads up — I'm telling the kids about Nico today and he'll be at the party") would have cost you nothing and taken the whole "I heard it from a 9-year-old" argument off the table. That's the same bar he met last April, and it's a low one. You cleared the hard part of this and tripped on the easy part.

That's a small miss, not a violation. But if you want to be taken seriously on the bigger stuff, it helps to own it cleanly rather than defend it.

**The double standard is real, and it's also a trap.** You have every right to notice that he's holding you to a standard he didn't meet. But "you did the same thing" will make him defensive, not reflective, and it turns this into a scorecard. The more useful framing is forward-looking: "Neither of us has been consistent about notice. Let's agree on what it looks like." You get the point across without having to win it.

**The Zara thing is the actual problem.** Repeatedly asking a 9-year-old whether your boyfriend sleeps over is not a parenting-plan question — it's using a kid to surveil you, and she felt it. That deserves its own conversation, separate from the party dispute, and it deserves to be raised calmly rather than as a counter-punch. "Zara told me she felt uncomfortable being asked about Nico. If you have questions about my household, ask me directly. I'll answer." That's hard to argue with.

**On your theory that it's really about you moving on.** You're probably at least partly right. It would be strange if there were zero feeling there. But it's unprovable, and saying it to him will end the conversation. You don't need him to admit the motive. You just need the behavior to stop.

**One last thing:** his Sunday-night lecture stung, and it was meant to. But "hearing about this from Zara felt bad" is a feeling you can acknowledge without conceding that you did anything wrong. "I get why that landed badly, and I should have sent you a heads-up that morning. The timing was within the plan, and I'd like us to agree on how we handle notice going forward" is a stronger position than either apologizing for the whole thing or defending every piece of it.

You've handled the substance of this well. Don't let the text-fight make you forget that.

Mostly, yes. On the things that matter:

- You didn't break the rule. Seven months is more than six.
- He did break it, at four.
- Questioning Zara about sleepovers was wrong, and it's the most serious thing anyone did here.
- Your instinct that his reaction is about more than the plan is probably accurate.

But I'd push back on the question itself. "Am I right" treats this as a case to be won, and if you walk into the next conversation with Graham holding a verdict, it'll go badly even though the verdict is mostly in your favor. The one thing you didn't do well — the heads-up text — is small, but it's real, and it's the only thing he can legitimately point to. If you concede it plainly, he has nothing left to stand on except the double standard and the interrogation of your daughter, both of which are his problems, not yours.

So: you're right about the substance. Being right isn't the same as the situation being handled. Those are the next steps, and you're in a strong position to take them.
